questions.q: What do the real, user, and sys values mean in the output of the command time ./app?
questions.hint: Distinguish between wall-clock time and CPU time in different modes.
options: real is elapsed physical time, user is CPU time in user code, sys is CPU time in kernel calls
real is disk operation time, user is keyboard input time, sys is OS system time
real is compilation time, user is execution time, sys is debugging time
real is memory time, user is processor time, sys is graphics card time
explanations: Correct! `real` is actual elapsed time ("wall-clock time"). `user` is total CPU time spent on program code. `sys` is CPU time spent by the kernel executing system calls for this program.
Incorrect. These are precise indicators of processor resource allocation.
Incorrect. `time` measures parameters of one specific process during execution.
Incorrect. The parameters describe only CPU and system time.

questions.q: What is the command objdump -d used for when analyzing a compiled C program?
questions.hint: The letter -d stands for disassemble.
options: To view assembly instructions of the machine code sections of an executable file
To strip the symbol table from a binary
To decompile machine code back into C source code
To check memory for leaks
explanations: Correct! `objdump -d` decompiles executable sections of an ELF binary file, allowing you to see actual machine instructions in assembly.
Incorrect. Symbol stripping is performed by the `strip` utility.
Incorrect. `objdump` outputs assembly code; it does not recreate C source code.
Incorrect. Memory leaks are checked by `Valgrind`.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Stripping Symbols with strip
questions.q: What does the strip command do to an application binary file?
questions.hint: Think about how to reduce the size of a final release file.
options: Removes the symbol table and debugging information to reduce file size
Compresses the binary file using the gzip algorithm
Deletes the executable file from disk permanently
Clears dynamic memory (heap) of the application
explanations: Correct! The `strip` utility removes symbol tables and DWARF debugging sections, which significantly reduces the size of an executable file or shared `.so` library before release.
Incorrect. `strip` does not use archiving or compression; it cuts out metadata.
Incorrect. Files are deleted using `rm`.
Incorrect. `strip` operates on a static file on disk, not runtime memory.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — ELF Section Size Analysis (size)
questions.q: What information is output by the console utility size ./app?
questions.hint: Recall standard ELF file sections: text, data, bss.
options: The sizes of the .text, .data, and .bss memory sections of the executable file in bytes
File size on disk taking all access permissions into account
Amount of allocated virtual memory at launch time
Number of lines of code in the project
explanations: Correct! The `size` utility outputs the size of the main segments of a binary file: `.text` (code), `.data` (initialized global data), and `.bss` (uninitialized data).
Incorrect. Disk size is shown by `ls -lh` or `stat`.
Incorrect. Dynamic memory consumption is measured by `top`, `ps`, or `valgrind`.
Incorrect. Lines of code are counted by `cloc` or `wc -l`.

questions.q: Which flag must be passed to GCC during build to later analyze C code performance via gprof?
questions.hint: This flag forces the compiler to inject code for collecting profiling info into gmon.out.
options: -pg
-profile
-gprof
explanations: Correct! The `-pg` flag embeds function call counters into the executable. Running the program generates a `gmon.out` file, which is then analyzed by `gprof`.
Incorrect. The `-profile` flag does not exist in GCC.
Incorrect. The utility name is `gprof`, but the compiler flag is `-pg`.
Incorrect. `-O3` sets the optimization level, not profiling.

questions.q: What does the -fsanitize=address option do when building a C program?
questions.hint: AddressSanitizer (ASan) catches memory errors right at runtime.
options: Embeds fast dynamic checking for out-of-bounds array access, use-after-free, and memory leaks at runtime
Optimizes address alignment in RAM
Encrypts pointers in the binary file
Checks code style compliance against PEP/MISRA standards
explanations: Correct! AddressSanitizer (ASan) replaces memory allocation calls and adds shadow memory checks, crashing with an instant intelligible report upon any out-of-bounds access or use-after-free.
Incorrect. ASan increases memory consumption and slightly slows down the program, but does not optimize it.
Incorrect. Encryption is not performed.
Incorrect. ASan works at program runtime, not with code style.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Translating Addresses to Code via addr2line
questions.q: Why do C developers use the addr2line console utility?
questions.hint: The name of the utility stands for Address to Line.
options: Translates a hexadecimal memory address from an error report into a C file and line number
Counts the total number of lines in memory addresses
Binds library addresses to network IP addresses
Formats source code into a single line
explanations: Correct! If debug symbols are present in a crashed program, `addr2line -e ./app 0x...` translates a virtual instruction address into a `.c` file name and exact line number.
Incorrect. The utility does not count lines of code in a project.
Incorrect. The utility works with DWARF symbols in ELF files.
Incorrect. It is a binary/DWARF debugging tool, not a text formatter.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Dry Run Build with make -n
questions.q: What does the -n (or --just-print) flag do when calling the make build system?
questions.hint: This flag is useful to see which commands make would execute.
options: Prints the commands that WOULD be executed to build, but does not execute them ("dry run")
Runs the build with parallel execution across N threads
Ignores all errors in the Makefile
Creates a new empty Makefile
explanations: Correct! `make -n` outputs the full chain of compiler and linker invocation commands to the console without actually running them. This helps debug the `Makefile` itself.
Incorrect. Parallel building is handled by the `-j` flag.
Incorrect. Error ignoring is done with the `-k` or `-i` flags.
Incorrect. `make -n` does not create files.

questions.q: What does the -j4 argument mean in the command make -j4?
questions.hint: The letter j stands for jobs.
options: Runs up to 4 parallel jobs (build tasks) simultaneously to speed up compilation
Sets compiler optimization to level 4
Builds only the 4th file from the list
Sets a 4 GB RAM limit for the build
explanations: Correct! The `-jN` flag sets the number of jobs executed concurrently (compiling independent `.c` files), which significantly speeds up builds on multi-core processors.
Incorrect. Optimization is controlled by compiler flags in the Makefile (e.g., `-O2`).
Incorrect. `-j4` does not select the 4th file in order.
Incorrect. The flag does not manage memory limits.

questions.topic: GDB CLI — Printing Arrays via Pointer
questions.q: What will the command (gdb) print *ptr@5 output in GDB if ptr is an int* pointer?
questions.hint: The @ symbol lets you specify the number of displayed elements in a contiguous array.
options: The first 5 elements of the array pointed to by ptr
The value of the 5th element of the array (ptr[5])
The value at address ptr multiplied by 5
A syntax error (@ operator is forbidden in GDB)
explanations: Correct! The `*ptr@len` construct in GDB allows printing an array of `len` elements starting from address `ptr`.
Incorrect. The fifth element is printed as `print ptr[4]` or `print *(ptr+4)`.
Incorrect. Multiplication uses standard `*`.
Incorrect. The `@` operator is a special GDB feature for working with memory via pointers.

questions.q: How does the command (gdb) watch counter differ from a standard (gdb) break?
questions.hint: A watchpoint responds to memory changes rather than reaching a line of code.
options: watch pauses program execution at the moment the value of variable counter CHANGES
watch pauses the program on the first READ of variable counter
watch tracks memory leaks of variable counter
watch removes variable counter from memory
explanations: Correct! A `watchpoint` stops the program immediately after a processor instruction changes the value in the tracked variable/memory region.
Incorrect. To track memory reads, `rwatch` (read watchpoint) is used.
Incorrect. GDB watchpoints do not look for memory leaks.
Incorrect. The command does not modify the program's memory structure.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Standalone Preprocessor Launch cpp
questions.q: What function does the cpp binary perform on a Linux system?
questions.hint: cpp is not C++, it is the C PreProcessor.
options: It is a standalone C preprocessor that substitutes #include and macros without invoking the compiler
It is a C++ compiler
It is a utility for checking C syntax
It is a package manager for C/C++ libraries
explanations: Correct! The `cpp` (C PreProcessor) command runs the C preprocessor directly. The output is processed text with expanded macros and inserted headers.
Incorrect. The C++ compiler is `g++` or `clang++`.
Incorrect. `cpp` performs text substitutions, not full syntax parsing.
Incorrect. Package managers include `conan`, `vcpkg`, or system apt/dnf.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Viewing Data Dump via xxd
questions.q: Why do C developers use utilities like xxd or hexdump?
questions.hint: Think about working with binary data files or non-text dumps.
options: To view the contents of binary files in hexadecimal (hex) and ASCII forms
To convert C code into HTML
To compress files into hex format
To encrypt program data
explanations: Correct! Utilities `xxd` and `hexdump` display raw bytes of binary files in a hex grid with parallel printable ASCII character output.
Incorrect. Code to HTML conversion is done by highlighters like `highlight`.
Incorrect. Hex representation increases size rather than compressing it.
Incorrect. The utility simply displays bytes.

questions.q: Why is sudo ldconfig run after copying a new .so library into the system directory /usr/local/lib?
questions.hint: How does the dynamic linker quickly find libraries without rescanning all folders?
options: Updates system dynamic library cache (/etc/ld.so.cache) so the loader can find them immediately
Compiles library source files into an object file
Scans the library for viruses
Restarts all running C applications
explanations: Correct! The dynamic linker `ld.so` reads the binary cache `/etc/ld.so.cache`. The `ldconfig` command scans system directories and updates this cache and symbolic links.
Incorrect. `ldconfig` does not compile code.
Incorrect. Security checking is done by antivirus software.
Incorrect. Processes are not restarted when updating `ldconfig` cache.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Changing RPATH via patchelf
questions.q: What is the patchelf tool used for when working with compiled binaries in Linux?
questions.hint: It allows modifying metadata of an existing ELF file.
options: Allows modifying RPATH and dynamic interpreter name in an existing ELF file without rebuilding
Automatically fixes bugs in C code
Patches the Linux kernel for faster system calls
Converts ELF binaries into Windows .exe format
explanations: Correct! The `patchelf` utility lets you modify header fields of existing ELF executables and `.so` files (e.g., changing dependency search path `RPATH` or interpreter `ld-linux.so`).
Incorrect. `patchelf` is unrelated to semantic bugs in source C code.
Incorrect. The utility works with user-space ELF files, not the kernel.
Incorrect. Running on Windows uses Wine or cross-compilation.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Symbol Demangling with c++filt
questions.q: Why might a C developer need c++filt when analyzing symbol tables?
questions.hint: When calling C++ libraries from C or in mixed compiled code, function names get mangled.
options: Decodes ("demangles") compiler-mangled symbol names (e.g., _Z3foov -> foo())
Converts C++ code into pure C
Filters string literals in a binary file
Removes C++ code from a C project
explanations: Correct! C++ compilers (and some C functions) mangle function names in the symbol table to support overloading. `c++filt` turns a mangled name back into a readable function signature.
Incorrect. It does not translate code.
Incorrect. Filtering strings is done with `grep` or `strings`.
Incorrect. `c++filt` only decodes text symbol strings.

questions.q: What problem does the Massif tool solve within Valgrind (--tool=massif)?
questions.hint: Massif plots memory usage over time.
options: Profiles RAM consumption (heap/stack) over time and produces peak call snapshots
Searches for data races in multithreaded programs (Data Races)
Checks GPU performance
Automatically frees unclosed dynamic memory
explanations: Correct! `Massif` is a heap profiler. It takes detailed snapshots of memory allocations during program execution and shows which functions allocated the most memory at peak.
Incorrect. Data races are searched using `Helgrind` or `DRD` in Valgrind.
Incorrect. Valgrind works with host CPU and memory.
Incorrect. Valgrind does not alter code behavior or call `free` for the programmer.

questions.q: What does the compiler flag -fsanitize=undefined detect?
questions.hint: UBSan detects atypical runtime behavior: signed int overflow, division by 0, etc.
options: Catches undefined behavior cases (signed overflow, division by 0, shifts by invalid bits) during program execution
Finds unused variables at compile time
Detects functions without return specifiers
Forbids code compilation if there is no main function
explanations: Correct! UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) inserts checks for runtime operations exceeding standard guarantees (signed integer overflow, null pointer dereference, misaligned pointer access).
Incorrect. Unused variables are detected by static flag `-Wunused-variable`.
Incorrect. Missing return check is set via `-Wreturn-type`.
Incorrect. This is checked by the linker by default.

questions.topic: GDB CLI — Batch Mode for CI/CD
questions.q: Why are gdb flags -batch -ex "bt" ./app core used in automated test scripts (CI/CD)?
questions.hint: The -batch flag disables interactive mode, while -ex executes a debug command.
options: To automatically extract a stack trace (backtrace) from a crashed program's core file to console and exit GDB immediately
To interactively connect to a crashed server
To force-restart a crashed program
To convert a core file into C text code
explanations: Correct! The `-batch` flag suppresses GDB's interactive prompt, `-ex "bt"` runs the call stack print command `backtrace` on the crashed `core` file and returns control to the pipeline immediately.
Incorrect. `-batch` excludes interactive user input.
Incorrect. GDB in this mode only reads a memory dump.
Incorrect. Source code is not restored from a `core` file.

questions.q: What can be learned by reading the virtual file /proc/$PID/maps of a running C program?
questions.hint: The maps file contains information on memory address segments of a process.
options: Process virtual memory allocation map (stack, heap addresses, loaded .so libraries, and access permissions)
All source `.c` files used by the program
History of commands entered by the user into the program
Passwords and encryption keys of the process
explanations: Correct! `/proc/$PID/maps` contains a full snapshot of the process address space: virtual address ranges, permissions (`rwxp`), offsets, and loaded dynamic modules.
Incorrect. Source C files are not contained in the kernel `/proc` virtual interface.
Incorrect. Input history is handled by other libraries (readline/bash history).
Incorrect. This file shows memory layout, not secret application data.

questions.q: Why does a C programmer use the command lsof -p <PID>?
questions.hint: lsof stands for List Open Files.
options: Shows all open files, network sockets, and pipes held by the specified process
Counts number of lines in project files
Forcefully closes process with specified PID
Clears disk cache of process
explanations: Correct! `lsof -p <PID>` outputs a list of all open file descriptors (including regular files, devices, network sockets, and FIFO pipes) used by the process. Useful for finding file descriptor leaks.
Incorrect. Line count is calculated with `wc`.
Incorrect. Terminating processes is done with `kill`.
Incorrect. Cache clearing is managed by the OS kernel.

questions.q: Is it true that -O0 disables GCC compiler optimizations, making code generation straightforward and convenient for step-by-step GDB debugging?
questions.hint: At -O0, machine code instructions strictly correspond to line order in C source.
options: True (-O0 disables optimizations, preventing line jumping during debugging)
False (-O0 enables maximum optimization level)
explanations: Correct! The `-O0` flag disables most code transformations. Variables are not evicted from memory into registers unnecessarily, and instruction order matches source C code.
Incorrect. Maximum standardized optimizations are enabled with `-O3` or `-Ofast`.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Function Interposition via LD_PRELOAD
questions.q: What happens when running a program with the LD_PRELOAD environment variable specified?
questions.hint: This variable specifies a priority library for the dynamic loader ld.so.
options: The dynamic loader loads the specified library before all others, allowing interception (hooking) of functions like malloc() or write()
The program is forcibly recompiled before execution
The loader raises a security error and completely blocks execution of the binary
explanations: Correct! `LD_PRELOAD` allows injecting your `.so` library with top priority. If function `malloc()` is declared in it, the loader will bind application calls to your implementation.
Incorrect. `LD_PRELOAD` works only at dynamic loading time upon startup without compilation.
Incorrect. The loader successfully runs the program (unless SUID mode is enabled for root-owned files).

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Determining Binary Parameters with file
questions.q: Which utility allows you to instantly inspect binary architecture (32/64-bit), linkage type (dynamically linked), and debug symbol status (stripped / not stripped)?
questions.hint: A simple system utility for determining file type by signature.
options: file ./app
cat ./app
stat ./app
type ./app
explanations: Correct! The `file` command analyzes Magic Numbers headers and outputs a detailed summary: `ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, with debug_info, not stripped`.
Incorrect. `cat` will simply output binary garbage on terminal.
Incorrect. `stat` shows permissions, file size, and timestamps (atime, mtime, ctime).
Incorrect. `type` shows whether a command is shell builtin or external file.

questions.q: Which GCC compiler flag forces all warnings to be treated as fatal errors, stopping compilation?
questions.hint: Used in CI/CD to enforce high code quality.
options: -Werror
-Wall
-Wextra
-Wfatal-errors
-Wpedantic
explanations: Correct! The `-Werror` flag instructs GCC to abort compilation if even a single warning occurs.
Incorrect. `-Wall` only enables a basic set of warnings.
Incorrect. `-Wextra` enables additional checks.
Incorrect. `-Wfatal-errors` stops compilation on the first ERROR, but does not turn warnings into errors.
Incorrect. `-Wpedantic` issues warnings for non-conformance to strict ISO C standard.

questions.q: Which signal is sent to a process by default when calling kill <PID> without extra flags?
questions.hint: This signal requests process to gracefully terminate (signal number 15).
options: SIGTERM (15)
SIGKILL (9)
SIGINT (2)
SIGSEGV (11)
SIGHUP (1)
SIGABRT (6)
explanations: Correct! The `kill PID` command sends the `SIGTERM` (15) signal, giving the program a chance to catch it, clean up resources, and exit gracefully.
Incorrect. `SIGKILL` (9) is sent when explicitly specifying `kill -9` or `kill -KILL`.
Incorrect. `SIGINT` (2) is usually sent via `Ctrl+C` shortcut.
Incorrect. `SIGSEGV` (11) is generated by kernel on memory protection violation.
Incorrect. `SIGHUP` (1) is sent when closing terminal.
Incorrect. `SIGABRT` (6) is triggered by `abort()` function or `assert()` failure.

questions.topic: GCC — Static Linking with Standard Library
questions.q: Is it true that when compiling a C program with the -static flag, the final executable includes all necessary libc functions (e.g., printf, malloc), and libc.so libraries are not required at runtime?
questions.hint: Static compilation embeds library code directly inside binary.
options: True (The file becomes standalone, but significantly larger in size)
False (Shared libraries are still loaded at runtime)
explanations: Correct! The `-static` flag tells the linker to embed all library code inside the binary itself. The application does not require external `.so` libraries, but increases in size.
Incorrect. Under dynamic linking, libraries are loaded via `ld.so`, but with `-static` dynamic loader is not used at all.

questions.topic: GDB CLI — Displaying Local Variables in All Stack Frames
questions.q: What does the bt full command do in the GDB debugger?
questions.hint: The bt (backtrace) command shows the call stack, and the full modifier expands output.
options: Prints function call stack (backtrace), displaying local variables in each stack frame
Restarts program debugging with full clearing of all breakpoints
Prints full disassembly of current function
explanations: Correct! `bt full` not only prints function names and line numbers of call stack, but also automatically outputs values of all local variables for each frame.
Incorrect. Restart is done with `run`, breakpoint clearing with `delete`.
Incorrect. Assembly code is printed with `disassemble`.

questions.q: Which utility creates a 'tags' index file for fast navigation to function definitions, structs, and data types in console editors (Vim/Emacs)?
questions.hint: The utility name contains the word tags.
options: ctags
gcc-index
objdump
grep
explanations: Correct! The `ctags` utility (or `exuberant-ctags` / `universal-ctags`) scans C files and creates an index table allowing Vim to jump to function declarations instantly upon cursor placement.
Incorrect. `gcc-index` utility does not exist in standard toolkit.
Incorrect. `objdump` works with compiled ELF files.
Incorrect. `grep` performs text search across files but does not generate index structures.

questions.q: Which compilation option must be passed to GCC so that executing the program generates statistical data files (.gcda/.gcno) for the gcov tool?
questions.hint: This flag enables generation of code coverage counting instructions.
options: --coverage (or -fprofile-arcs -ftest-coverage)
-fPIC -shared
-fsanitize=address
-g -O3
-pg
explanations: Correct! The `--coverage` flag instruments code so execution creates line call statistics for subsequent coverage analysis via `gcov` / `lcov`.
Incorrect. `-fPIC -shared` are used for building dynamic libraries.
Incorrect. `-fsanitize=address` activates ASan for finding memory errors.
Incorrect. `-g -O3` include debug symbols and maximum optimization.
Incorrect. `-pg` is used for call time profiling via `gprof`.

questions.topic: Linux CLI — Redirecting stdout and stderr to Single File
questions.q: Which construct in Bash shell combines and redirects BOTH standard output (stdout) AND error stream (stderr) to file log.txt?
questions.hint: Modern Bash uses the compact operator &>.
options: ./app &> log.txt (or ./app > log.txt 2>&1)
./app 2> log.txt
./app < log.txt
./app 1>&2 log.txt
./app | log.txt
./app >> log.txt 0>&1
explanations: Correct! Syntax `&> log.txt` (or classic `> log.txt 2>&1`) redirects both file descriptors (1 and 2) into one specified file.
Incorrect. `2> log.txt` redirects ONLY errors (stderr).
Incorrect. `< log.txt` passes file to standard input (stdin).
Incorrect. `1>&2` redirects stdout to stderr.
Incorrect. `|` creates a pipe to pass stream to another program, not a file.
Incorrect. `0>&1` binds input to standard output.
